paragraphs: It is a just observation, and not a new one, that enemies of particular persons and opponents of particular measures seldom confine their criticism to what actually deserves blame in either. Only on this principle is it easy to explain the motives of those who condemn the proposed Constitution as a whole and treat with severity some of its most unobjectionable articles.
The second section gives power to the President, "BY AND WITH THE ADVICE AND CONSENT OF THE SENATE, TO MAKE TREATIES, PROVIDED TWO THIRDS OF THE SENATORS PRESENT CONCUR."

The power of making treaties is an important one, especially as it bears on war, peace and commerce. It should be delegated only in a way, and with such precautions, as will give the highest security that it will be exercised by the men best qualified for it, and in the manner most conducive to the public good. The Convention appears to have attended to both points. It has directed that the President be chosen by select bodies of electors, appointed by the people for that express purpose, and it has committed the appointment of senators to the State legislatures. In such cases this method has a vast advantage over elections by the people in their collective capacity. In those elections the activity of party zeal, taking advantage of the indifference, the ignorance, and the hopes and fears of the unwary and the interested, often puts men in office by the votes of a small proportion of the electors.

The select assemblies that choose the President, like the State legislatures that appoint the senators, will in general be composed of the most enlightened and respectable citizens. There is reason to presume, therefore, that they will direct their attention and their votes only to those men who have become most distinguished for their abilities and virtue, and in whom the people see just grounds for confidence. The Constitution shows very particular attention to this object. It excludes men under thirty-five from the first office and those under thirty from the second. In this way it confines the electors to men of whom the people have had time to form a judgment, and with respect to whom they will not be liable to be deceived by those brilliant displays of talent and patriotism which, like passing meteors, sometimes mislead as well as dazzle. If it is well founded to say that wise kings will always be served by able ministers, it is fair to argue that an assembly of select electors has, in a greater degree than kings, the means of broad and accurate information about men and characters, and so their appointments will show at least equal discretion and discernment. The natural inference from these considerations is that the President and senators so chosen will always be among those who best understand our national interests, whether in relation to the individual States or to foreign nations; who are best able to promote those interests; and whose reputation for integrity inspires and deserves confidence. With such men the power of making treaties may safely be lodged.

The absolute necessity of system in the conduct of any business is universally known and acknowledged. Yet its great importance in national affairs has not yet been sufficiently impressed on the public mind. Those who wish to commit the power under consideration to a popular assembly, made up of members constantly coming and going in quick succession, seem not to recall that such a body must be inadequate to attaining the great objects that need to be kept steadily in view in all their relations and circumstances. Those objects can be approached and achieved only by measures that require not only talents but also exact information, and often much time, to plan and to carry out. It was wise, therefore, for the Convention to provide not only that the power of making treaties should be committed to able and honest men, but also that they should stay in place long enough to become perfectly acquainted with our national concerns, and to form and introduce a system for managing them. The term prescribed is such as will give them an opportunity to greatly extend their political information, and to make their accumulating experience more and more beneficial to their country. The Convention has shown no less prudence in providing for the frequent election of senators in a way that avoids the problem of periodically handing these great affairs over entirely to new men. By leaving a considerable remainder of the old ones in place, it preserves uniformity and order, as well as a constant succession of official information.

Few will deny that trade and navigation should be governed by a system that is carefully designed and steadily followed, and that our treaties and our laws alike should fit that system and be made to advance it. It matters greatly that this fit be carefully maintained. Anyone who grants the point will see and admit that it is well secured by making the agreement of the Senate necessary to both treaties and laws.

It seldom happens in negotiating treaties, of whatever kind, that perfect SECRECY and immediate DISPATCH are not sometimes required. These are cases where the most useful intelligence may be obtained, if the persons who possess it can be relieved of the fear of discovery. That fear will affect those persons whether they act from mercenary or from friendly motives, and there are doubtless many of both kinds who would rely on the secrecy of the President but would not trust that of the Senate, and still less that of a large popular assembly. The Convention has done well, therefore, in arranging the power of making treaties so that, although the President must act by the advice and consent of the Senate in forming them, he will be able to manage the business of intelligence as prudence may suggest.

Those who have turned their attention to the affairs of men must have noticed that there are tides in them: tides very irregular in their duration, strength and direction, and seldom found to run twice in exactly the same manner or measure. To discern these tides in national affairs and profit by them is the business of those who preside over those affairs. Those who have had much experience in this field tell us that there are often occasions when days, indeed even hours, are precious. The loss of a battle, the death of a prince, the removal of a minister, or other circumstances that change the present posture and look of affairs may turn the most favorable tide into a course opposite to our wishes. As in the field, so in the cabinet, there are moments to be seized as they pass, and those who preside in either should be left able to make use of them. So often and so seriously have we suffered in the past from lack of secrecy and dispatch that the Constitution would have been inexcusably defective if it had paid no attention to those objects. The matters that usually require the most secrecy and the most dispatch in negotiations are the preparatory and auxiliary measures, which matter from the national point of view only because they help to reach the objects of the negotiation. For these the President will have no difficulty making provision. And should any circumstance arise that requires the advice and consent of the Senate, he may convene them at any time. Thus we see that the Constitution provides for our negotiations of treaties to have every advantage that can be drawn from talents, information, integrity and deliberate investigation on the one hand, and from secrecy and dispatch on the other.
But to this plan, as to most others that have ever appeared, objections are devised and pressed.

Some are unhappy with it, not because they find any error or defect in it, but because treaties, once made, are to have the force of laws, and so, they say, should be made only by men who hold legislative authority. These gentlemen seem not to consider that the judgments of our courts, and the commissions our governor constitutionally issues, are as valid, and as binding on all the persons they concern, as the laws passed by our legislature. All constitutional acts of power, whether in the executive or in the judicial department, have as much legal validity and obligation as if they came from the legislature. Therefore, whatever name is given to the power of making treaties, and however binding treaties may be when made, it is certain that the people may with much propriety commit that power to a body distinct from the legislative, the executive or the judicial. It surely does not follow that because they have given the power of making laws to the legislature, they should likewise give it the power to do every other act of sovereignty by which the citizens are to be bound and affected.

Others, though content that treaties should be made in the way proposed, object to their being the SUPREME laws of the land. They insist, and profess to believe, that treaties, like acts of assembly, should be repealable at pleasure. This idea seems to be new and peculiar to this country, but new errors, as well as new truths, often appear. These gentlemen would do well to reflect that a treaty is only another name for a bargain. It would be impossible to find a nation that would make any bargain with us that bound it ABSOLUTELY but bound us only so long and so far as we might think proper. Those who make laws may, without doubt, amend or repeal them, and it will not be disputed that those who make treaties may alter or cancel them. But let us not forget that treaties are made, not by only one of the contracting parties, but by both. Consequently, just as the consent of both was essential to their formation at first, so it must always be afterward for altering or canceling them. The proposed Constitution, therefore, has not in the least extended the obligation of treaties. They are just as binding, and just as far beyond the lawful reach of legislative acts, now as they will be at any future time or under any form of government.

However useful jealousy may be in republics, when it abounds too much in the body politic, like bile in the natural body, the eyes of both become very liable to be deceived by the false appearances that this malady casts on surrounding objects. This is probably the source of the fears and suspicions of some, that the President and Senate may make treaties without an equal eye to the interests of all the States. Others suspect that two thirds will oppress the remaining third. They ask whether these gentlemen are made sufficiently responsible for their conduct; whether, if they act corruptly, they can be punished; and, if they make disadvantageous treaties, how we are to get rid of those treaties.

All the States are equally represented in the Senate, and by men who are the most able and the most willing to promote the interests of their constituents. They will therefore all have an equal degree of influence in that body, especially while they continue to take care in appointing proper persons and to insist on their punctual attendance. In proportion as the United States take on a national form and a national character, the good of the whole will be more and more an object of attention. A government would have to be weak indeed to forget that the good of the whole can be promoted only by advancing the good of each of the parts or members that make up the whole. It will not be in the power of the President and Senate to make any treaties by which they and their families and estates will not be bound and affected equally with the rest of the community. And since they have no private interests distinct from that of the nation, they will be under no temptation to neglect the latter.

As for corruption, we cannot even suppose it. Anyone who thinks it likely that the President and two thirds of the Senate will ever be capable of such unworthy conduct must have been very unlucky in his dealings with the world, or have a heart all too ready to believe the worst. The idea is too gross and too odious to be entertained. But in such a case, if it should ever happen, the treaty so obtained from us would, like all other fraudulent contracts, be null and void by the law of nations.

As for their responsibility, it is hard to see how it could be increased. Every consideration that can influence the human mind affords security for their fidelity: honor, oaths, reputation, conscience, love of country, and family affections and attachments. In short, the Constitution has taken the utmost care that they shall be men of talents and integrity. So we have reason to be persuaded that the treaties they make will be as advantageous as, all circumstances considered, could be made. And as far as the fear of punishment and disgrace can operate, that motive to good behavior is amply provided by the article on impeachments.
